mr president, ladies and gentlemen, these elections are taking place at the most critical moment in the european union's existence. that's good, because now we need another alternative, a better one for europe. after a long series of political, economic, migration and security crises, we must recognise that the brexit referendum was the first serious warning to the union. the union is teetering on the edge of a precipice. britain will leave, supported by president-elect trump. in the last few days, i and the other candidates have also released a series of documents in which we have outlined our reasons for running, our recommendations, our beliefs and the visions we want to put into practice. there is an obsession with political correctness, which leads to a lack of courage in clearly pointing out both the real causes and the obvious solutions for parliament and the citizens of our countries. if we really believe that the european union is in a deep crisis, then it is obvious that a superficial change will not be enough. no, i think it's not enough and please look closer and closer. the old speeches and routine actions don't work anymore. the europe of nations and freedoms group, which i represent, is calling for more democracy and more transparency in the european parliament. we demand respect for the millions of taxpayers who voted for our candidates, we demand respect for the rights of our mps in committees and delegations and we demand an end to the administrative harassment to which our political staff members are subjected. if this is a democratic institution, then why is it not allowed such a simple thing as giving a seat in the front row to our president? i ask for balance and fairness for all members, because democracy and respect cannot be the preserve of the big groups. we reject any affiliation, connection or sympathy, present or future, with any authoritarian or totalitarian regime. we all want parliament to play a bigger role. but first let us ask ourselves how the relationship with the european commission, which has consistently shown a lack of respect for parliament, really worked. we, the europe of nations and freedoms group, oppose any transfer of national sovereignty to any supranational institution. we want a europe of cooperation, which respects the interests of our nations. moreover, i believe that the strength of nations lies in the preservation and development of their specificities. and last but not least, we must defend inside and outside this chamber, individual freedom, freedom of speech and digital freedom. but back to the main question: what kind of president do we really want for the european parliament? some say we need a strong president, able to impose political will. but how fair would it be to impose such a will? others believe that it is not the president who should be strong, but parliament itself. but i wonder how parliament could act coherently and innovatively if it is dominated by political groups dictating an agenda? even if we don't share the same vision, we need stability. we need the patience and will of a president who can ensure that parliamentary rules and compromises are respected. whoever he is, the president must be fair, patient in negotiations and strong in decision-making to defend stability and fairness for all mps. at the same time, it will have to defend parliament's interests vis-à-vis all the other institutions. ladies and gentlemen, i call on you to vote for real change, based on transparent and coherent reform of this house. that was before we thought of any other form of union. people want a europe of nations and freedom, built on cooperation. we have to make the change in the name of the citizens and peace. i call on you to vote for the project i support and for a real democracy, extended and shared by all political groups and all members of the european parliament. real change never comes from outside, it has to come from within each one of us. and it could start any minute. may this day be the beginning of change!

in writing. we need a financial transaction tax as soon as possible to start taking direct action to prevent tax fraud, avoid double taxation and reduce distortions of competition in the european single market. only through joint action can we limit abuses and call for g20 global action. the taxation would thus be carried out at the place where the financial institution involved in the transaction is established, thus having an inhibitory effect on the process of delocalisation and bringing a real surplus to the budgets of the european union. with an estimated rate of 0.1% for equities and bonds and 0.01% for other types of transactions such as derivatives, the tax could generate revenues of approximately eur 57 billion per year. the european parliament therefore considers that this resource can feed the european budget in the future. the delay in the implementation of the levy reduces the european union's ability to implement common policy objectives. i therefore call on all institutional actors to speed up this process, which would increase transparency and strengthen citizens' confidence that the european union is an additional factor of development, and not an organisation financed entirely from national budgets.

the next item is the debate on the report of ms maria joão rodrigues, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the european pillar of social rights (2016/2095 (ini)) (a80391/2016).
mr president, while i commend the report for pointing out the vast number of social challenges eu countries are faced with, i find that it misjudged the causes of problems and consequently insists on the wrong solution. the issue is not that the eu is not social enough. i would point out that the eu accounts for approximately 7% of the world’s population but around 40% of global public social expenditure. existing social challenges are not so much a result of missing social policy but mainly of insufficient reforms, including to the labour market, and the lack of economic growth and job creation. a more social europe should not be one that throws money at every problem it identifies, or one that stifles competitiveness – a precondition for job creation and sustainable social protection. rather, in full respect for subsidiarity, it should be one that promotes sound economic policies and encourages national reforms in areas such as education and active labour market policies.

in writing. currently, eu member states are facing social and employment challenges, but also a continuous evolution of this market, with atypical or non-standard forms of employment: temporary or part-time work, seasonal work or work mediated by digital platforms. in addition, we are seeing a diversification of the workforce, which can bring benefits and generate other career opportunities, but can also generate drawbacks - prolonged economic insecurity, precarious working conditions, lower and less secure incomes, lack of social and health insurance, lack of career prospects and difficulties in reconciling work and family life. i therefore believe that more appropriate and more substantial strategic investment is needed to achieve the eu's social and employment objectives, but also more substantial support for cohesion in disadvantaged regions, with a view to making them more competitive and preventing further demographic decline, with a focus on reducing child poverty, and concrete measures to ensure access to free healthcare, education, decent housing and adequate food.
in writing. the european union needs a european pillar of social rights. but this social pillar must include a small number of social rights regulated at european level. in essence, social rights and policies must be the decision-making power of each member state. we consider that the determinants of social rights and policies are specific to each member state: demographic trends, level of economic development, traditions in social policies, etc. i believe that what is desired to be defined at european level goes far beyond what is necessary.
in writing. in the context of sustainable development and exponential change in all socio-economic areas, the european union must take swift and visible responsibility for the growing inequalities that have emerged in the european community, the increase in unemployment, work-life imbalances, poverty among children, young people and the elderly, and the systems needed to maintain health, security and human dignity. this is especially true given that, globally, the european union has high standards (not only) in social assistance and labour. this is because the developed european social model is the most advanced in world history, which gives and confers on the european union the leadership role in the field of social rights. it is therefore welcome to reflect on the existing social acquis, bringing together national parliaments, governments, eu institutions, civil society and social partners to develop a social rights pillar that addresses social protection and social services in an integrated way. clearly, the implementation of such a pillar requires instruments (including financial), public social investment, mechanisms, legislation and policies converging with economic, social and employment ones, so as to lead to an increase in the well-being of each european entity (especially employees and workers with typical employment contracts).

mr president, commissioner, the practice of genital mutilation is a serious form of violence against women and girls, an unacceptable violation of their right to bodily integrity. such practices should never be justified by religion, culture or tradition. commissioner, i welcome the commission's commitment to facilitating the exchange of experience and good practice on genital mutilation issues between member states. the use of eu funds to prevent these practices plays a vital role in protecting women and girls, identifying victims and taking action to combat them. the prevention of genital mutilation is an international human rights obligation for each member state and requires a firm approach and utmost vigilance to combat such practices.
in writing. female genital mutilation constitutes a violation of the fundamental right of girls and women to life, to safety, to dignity, to equality between women and men, to non-discrimination and to physical and emotional integrity. globally, it is estimated that between 100 million and 140 million girls and women have been subjected to some form of female genital mutilation, and if current trends continue, an additional 15 million girls aged 15 to 19 will be subjected to this cruelty by 2030. it is essential that the european executive and the eeas include the issue of female genital mutilation in the annual eu dialogues with civil society organisations in partner countries where the practice exists and continue to promote the provision of international protection to women at risk of female genital mutilation worldwide, in their relations with third countries and in international fora. close collaboration with the african union and the african group at the un is also needed to adopt new initiatives to strengthen the global fight against fgm and to support capacity building initiatives of public and civil society organisations.
in writing. according to the world health organization, about four million girls are subjected to female genital mutilation each year. this practice is part of local cultural rituals and customs in various communities or countries in africa and the middle east, but unfortunately it continues to exist even in places where it is prohibited by national legislation. more action is needed from the european commission. it must make development aid conditional on developing countries' efforts to eliminate this barbaric practice. today, i ask the commission to pay particular attention to cases occurring on the territory of the member states and to work closely with local and national authorities to firmly combat this practice. no girl living in the eu should be subjected to female genital mutilation.

the question is "blue cardboard". mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the main objective is to promote the rights of the child and that is also the subject of my question. don't you think the adoption process is very long? i therefore believe that there is a need for closer cooperation between national authorities to implement this important report.
mr president, the subject of adoption has become an increasingly important one with the increase in the mobility of people. the report comes up with a solution by proposing the development of common minimum standards for adoptions. although they are considered to be rather guidelines of good practice, all parties recognise that any adoption decision must be made solely in the best interests of the child and analysed in the light of individual characteristics. the report states that, at european level, biological parents should be given the right to have recourse to all legal remedies before adoption proceedings are commenced. this could make some problems between member states or even with third countries more transparent and ensure measures to protect children. in these circumstances, cases such as the barbu family in the uk or the bugnariu family in a third country such as norway will be treated with greater clarity, all the more so as the report indicates the need for the competent consular authorities to be kept informed of any proposed adoption decision in relation to a child who is a national of another member state, but most importantly that the rights of children will be protected.
member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, giving priority to the interests of the child may be found in international law and in member states’ law, and to that end it is necessary to consider two things: that these interests be properly translated into the procedural rules, because they should not be unnecessarily bureaucratic and lengthy; and also how they are applied. that is why i am in favour of doing much more in conjunction with the member states, for instance in the field of training of judges and professionals. the commission will consider adding this as a new topic amongst other topics: where we train judges on victims’ rights, procedural safeguards for children, brussels iia, etc., this could also be covered. so this is my commitment to you from today’s discussion. on the new legislation: family law is the domain of the member states. we must be very careful here because these are emotional and sensitive topics; unanimity is required for a very good reason. so we will consider this call for legislation, but, as i said before, it must be evidence-based, there must be a test of whether this is a severe pan-european problem; whether there is strong demand from the member states that we have a european solution; and the third important thing is whether the european union has any legal competence to regulate on this.
in writing. investing in children is an investment in the future of our society, and raising and educating them in decent and safe conditions must be a constant concern for everyone, no matter where they are. in this context, we are talking about cross-border adoptions and the best interests of the child in such situations. child protection is a priority in all situations and in the case of cross-border adoptions there are a number of factors that need to be taken into account to ensure that the best interests of children are protected. i support the importance of developing common minimum standards for adoption, but also the need for better civil justice cooperation in the field of adoption. since there is no binding framework at european level for the recognition of adoption decisions following a national procedure, legislative action is necessary to ensure that the right of european citizens to family life and to freedom of movement is respected at all times. the commission and the council must identify mechanisms to guarantee the protection of the interests of children, european citizens, even when they live outside the european union. it is extremely important that in such situations children have the opportunity to stay in touch with their cultural background, to learn and to use their mother tongue.
in writing. i would like to emphasise that the area of family law at national level, and therefore adoption, is a matter for the member states. however, when people decide to move to another member state of the union, difficulties arise in relation to the recognition and legal settlement of their legal status. however, i do not see why we need to create new legislation, to impose new rules, instead of using the levers we already have, to counter-interest member states to reach a uniform approach to adoption. on the one hand, the training of national officials and judges involved in adoptions, the exchange of experience and the improvement of cooperation between them should be supported. on the other hand, member states should be encouraged to avoid unnecessary red tape in the field of adoption. let's not forget that what should come first is the best interest of the child. in each of our countries there are enough abandoned children. it is important that each member state facilitates national procedures so that these children can fully enjoy all their rights, and above all the right to have a family.
in writing. every child in the world has the right to a family and an environment in which to be loved and to receive the education necessary for adult life. i therefore believe that the european institutions have a moral responsibility to protect the rights of every family and i am pleased that parliament is the first to propose a set of measures for those who have adopted children and want to enjoy the freedom to settle in a country other than their own. in the context of the ever-increasing number of international couples and families, community legislation must adapt to the new realities and give every family in europe the guarantee that its rights will be recognised and respected by the authorities in all member states. it is also regrettable that the european executive has not yet responded to the 2011 call of the ep to take measures to regulate cross-border adoption issues. this is not just about defending principles, but also about protecting the rights of all parents and children in the european union, wherever they are, in concrete situations.

madam president, providing enough quality food for a global population that is estimated to reach nearly 10 billion by 2050 will be a significant challenge. already demand is putting major pressure on limited natural resources, and competition for arable land is stimulating deforestation. climate forecasts show that arable land will also be threatened by other phenomena, such as changes in rainfall or the more pronounced impact of pests associated with higher temperatures. in this context, we urgently need solutions, we need more detailed research on low-risk pesticides and better procedures for their approval to be placed on the market. current procedures are too slow, forcing farmers to resort to conventional pesticides with all the implicit risks to health and the environment. alternative solutions, including plant protection products of biological origin and other biological control methods, could also support organic farmers and low-impact agriculture in general. many organic producers still have great difficulties in accessing european funds due to still complicated procedures. the accessibility of low-risk pesticides would be an indirect support measure that would benefit both them and consumers.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice—president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, once again i am stepping in on behalf of vice-president/high representative mogherini since she was indisposed and could not be here today. thank you for focusing your attention once again on the situation in the west bank and particularly on settlements. the international context may be evolving, but the european union’s position is not bound to change. we still believe that the only possible solution is the two-state solution, and we still believe that the current settlement policy, including the regularisation law, threatens the viability of the two states. you heard it directly from the high representative last november and then again during the debate in the committee on foreign affairs with eu special representative fernando gentilini and the french special envoy pierre vimont. we still believe in what the middle east quartet wrote last summer, that the two-state solution is in great danger, and urgent action is needed to stop and reverse the current trends. the quartet identified three major threats against the viability of the two states. first, continued settlement expansion, demolitions and the denial of palestinian development. second, violence and incitement to violence which inflict terrible suffering and deepen the mistrust between the communities, and third, the dire situation in gaza, the continued militant activity and the lack of palestinian unity. it is very clear that the situation is not improving and on some issues it is deteriorating. last november the high representative said in this hemicycle that the regularisation bill, if approved, would contradict very openly the quartet’s recommendations. consistent with this position, at the beginning of february we condemned the new israeli settlement announcements and the adoption of the regularisation law by the knesset. with this new law, the israeli parliament has legislated on the legal status of land within the occupied palestinian territory, which is an issue that remains beyond its jurisdiction. should it be implemented, the law would further entrench a one-state reality, a reality of unequal rights, perpetual occupation and conflict. for these reasons, the high representative has called on israel to refrain from implementing the law. on 8 february the high representative discussed the situation in a phone call with palestinian president mahmoud abbas. she told him that the european union will continue to work with the two parties, but also with international and regional partners, on the two-state solution. this is the only way to end the conflict and move the peace process forward. in fact, as we face such a difficult situation on the ground, it is essential to preserve international unity both on the fundamental coordinates of the two-state solution and on the way to get there. international unity has led the quartet’s report. international unity has led the un security council resolution 2334 last december, which condemned the israeli settlements in the occupied palestinian territory and reaffirmed that the 1967 lines can only be modified through an agreement between the parties. resolution 2334 also condemned all acts of incitement, violence and terror and called on both sides to take steps to advance the two-state solution on the ground in line with the recommendations of the quartet report. such consensus was confirmed at the middle east peace conference in paris on 15 january and the need for international unity was also central to the discussion in the last two foreign affairs councils. just days ago, high representative mogherini headed to the united states for a first round of meetings with the new administration. she met among others with secretary of state rex tillerson, national security adviser michael flynn, and the president’s senior adviser jared kushner. with all of them the high representative stressed that the quartet report must continue to be the bedrock of international action concerning the israeli-palestinian issue. she also stressed very clearly, in line with the messages conveyed also by leaders from the region, that any move of the us embassy to jerusalem could have a very negative and destabilising impact in the entire middle east at a time when the region needs all the stability it can get. she confirmed that the european union stands by the international consensus on jerusalem embodied in united nations security council resolution 478 of 1980. it is clear that the new us administration is still in the process of defining its foreign policy. we have a duty then to engage with them on the basis of our values and our interests, working to preserve international unity and to avoid any inflammatory moves. the situation in the region is incredibly delicate and fragile. a peaceful solution to this conflict, or even progress in that direction, could set a whole new paradigm for cooperation in the region, including on security. so our regional partners can play a major role in promoting a solution. the arab peace initiatives provide key elements for a comprehensive settlement of the conflict, and we hope that we can develop even further the cooperation between the european union and the arab league, and between the quartet and the arab states. the current lack of a peace process is no excuse for not trying. there are things that both sides can do today independently of each other that would advance a peaceful two-state reality on the ground. so it is essential to say loud and clear that we do not give up. the european union and the world do not give up on peace between the israelis and the palestinians. we simply cannot afford for tensions to rise again.

mr president, this week we are witnessing several fundamental debates about the future of economic and monetary union and the shape of the european economy. the main question is what we can do to strengthen the economy of the european union. the answer is that every member state of the european union has to have a stronger economy in order to make the economy of the union as a whole much stronger. member states have to converge, and they have to converge towards the level of the strongest and most competitive members. how can we achieve this in practice? firstly, the implementation of structural reforms, as outlined in the country—specific recommendations, is essential. only 4% of country—specific recommendations are fully implemented, and more than 50% are not implemented at all. we have to support member states in order to improve on the implementation of the country—specific recommendations and we have to find incentives for member states to implement the reforms which we all know that they need, and which are written in the country—specific recommendations, but which are not yet implemented well enough. to strengthen our economies so that they can face the next crisis, improving their competitiveness and reforming is the best recipe. the second element is trust. what improves trust in the union’s economy is its predictability and credibility. in this sense, respecting existing financial rules – the two-pack, six-pack and stability and growth pact – is of the essence.

madam president, we have reached the final stage of a lengthy and difficult process of exercising democratic scrutiny over the negotiation and approval of ceta. the s&d group has followed closely, as have many colleagues in this house, the negotiations since before what i would call its first conclusion in september 2014. we have voiced concerns, demanded changes and achieved most of those already on the occasion of what was effectively the second conclusion of the negotiations in february 2016. the most important of these was the removal of the old, toxic, isds from the treaty and its replacement with a public system, the new ics. in the past year, we have also contributed to, and closely scrutinised and debated, what became the new ceta package submitted to the european parliament for consent today. we welcome, as a group, the fact that many of the citizens’ concerns have been addressed through clarifications and commitments from the commission and the canadian authorities, through the joint interpretative instrument and the other instruments in the package. ceta is not perfect, far from it, but it is an important step in the right direction: a more progressive trade policy where the benefits are widely spread among all citizens. the s&d group has tabled its own consensual resolution which clarifies what we mean by progressive trade agreements by spelling out clearly what we like about ceta, and what we do not like about ceta and expect to be further corrected in ceta where agreed, or in future trade agreements more widely: better provisions on sustainable development and a sanctions-based approach; further improvements to the ics system and full european parliament involvement in the designation of judges; better forms to cover the protection of public services; and improved transparency for all trade agreements in future. the s&d group has decided to vote in favour of ceta. this is because most of us believe ceta is good for our economy, particularly for smes, and it does not threaten our choices, values or laws. but it is also an act of trust and an offer of partnership towards the eu institutions, notably the commission and the council, with which we want to work together for a better trade policy, and towards canada, which is a country that shares our values, our objectives and our hopes for a better future.
madam president, we need to protect european industries and european farmers and to support and protect our smes, start-ups and exporters. we also need to protect and promote our service industries, innovation and european ipr. i believe that there is a broad consensus on this both inside and outside this house. but how can we achieve this? is protectionism the best protection that we can provide? the history of the global economy and trade in the last hundred years teaches us that protectionism is a poor tool. the cost of protectionist measures has always turned out to be higher than the short—term gain of such measures. the best we can do for european industries, smes and farmers is to actively promote their interests. today that means providing for a fair, modern, 21st century trade agreement with a like—minded partner. today that means approving ceta.
madam president, commissioner, this is a historic moment for the european union, because it is the first free trade agreement that the european union has concluded with another major economy in the oecd. personally, i believe in the need for trade agreements with other non-european countries, but obviously on a win-win basis. the internal market needs to develop, to internationalise its businesses, especially smes. whenever you make a deal, you have to think about what you're losing and what you're gaining. you can't pretend to win all by yourself. that is why i support trade agreements, alongside trade defence measures and that is the commission's duty. my fears at the start of the negotiations were dispelled, those about product standards and the legal mechanism. in the end, we have to make an economic decision, but also a political one, and we always have to know which is the best option, because there is no ideal solution. so i think we have a duty to support the development of the internal market through good trade agreements, not to close the internal market.
mr president, ceta is a landmark free trade agreement that would make both parties richer. by abolishing 98% of tariffs and other trade barriers, it would provide excellent opportunities for smes. it would also liberalise cross-border investment and trade in services. it would open competition for large government contracts, it would support enforcement of intellectual property rights and would facilitate mutual recognition in the extremely important services market. beyond the merits of the agreement itself, its adoption would also signify two essential things. it would reinforce that the eu still believes in the benefits of free trade and open markets that ensured its post-war prosperity, and that it is able to regain some of the trade negotiation credibility that it lost when it decided to give up its exclusive competence over the deal.

the reporter. madam president, if we want security within the european union, then we must secure the external borders of the european union and that is what we have done with this regulation, a joint regulation of the european parliament and the council, by which we strengthen the external borders, we strengthen checks at the external borders of the european union. in short, what this proposal for a regulation brings is the verification of persons entering and leaving the european union, at any external border of the european union, in databases - and i will refer to this immediately: in databases. this is a change from today's situation where eu citizens are not checked on entering and leaving the schengen area, and non-eu citizens from third countries are only checked on entering and not on leaving. so what we're changing is that everyone, both eu citizens and non-eu citizens, will be checked both on entry and on exit, and we're not just talking about the schengen area, but the entire european union, so the external border of the european union. will they be checked how? they'll be checked against the databases. the compulsory databases to be checked by the member states are, according to this proposal for a regulation, the schengen information system and the interpol lost and stolen documents database. it also provides for verification in any other relevant european database. it could be the visa database or, in the future, because it has not yet been adopted, the exit database of people entering or leaving the european union. of course, these databases must be full of complete, accurate information and must be transmitted immediately by the member states. here again, i call on the member states, that all this cooperation and all this construction that we are doing depends on the speed and accuracy of the data that they send to the databases, because the member states are the ones who feed the databases, so they have a great responsibility to send the information quickly, completely and correctly. there are also some exceptions to the individual check, just to avoid making it more difficult to cross the border. for land and sea borders, it is possible that at any time, when there is a very high level of passenger traffic, those crossing the border may be asked to carry out targeted checks based on information, so that only certain persons are checked, only certain persons for whom information exists are checked in databases. this can of course be done with the agreement of the commission and after a risk assessment. for air borders there is a transition period of six months, during which member states are obliged to purchase all the necessary equipment for these checks, equipment and training of persons working at airports. this have to prove that you still have structural problems and technical problems. i'd like to give you an example of how this control will be done, so that everyone can understand. it's basically a scan other checks. so this isn't a random search of the databases. there's only one interface where you get a red flag if you find that name in one of the databases mentioned, which means it shouldn't take member of the commission. – mr president, i have listened to members’ comments and opinions with great interest and i am grateful for this rich exchange of views. this debate shows we share the aim of helping patients gain access to truly innovative medicines at affordable prices across the european union. i would like to pick up a couple of points raised in your report and in the debate. i support member states’ initiatives to help reduce medicine prices and increase transparency in the setting of such prices. small countries have lower negotiating power and face particular difficulties. i welcome the ongoing cooperation amongst european union countries in this regard. in addition, our european union joint procurement agreement enables member states to buy medicines together under the same conditions. in fact, most member states will buy pandemic vaccines together this year. thinking about vaccines, vaccine shortages are indeed a major challenge. this is why we are setting up a joint action on vaccines with the member states to help them forecast and manage vaccine needs. last and most important, the report provides a contribution to our ongoing work on health technology assessment. once again, my aim is to come up with a proposal that has clear benefits for all, including, above all, european patients. finally, i fully agree with the need for a strategic breakthrough on disease prevention to reduce the need for medicines, as expressed in your report. let me conclude by expressing again my gratitude to ms cabezón ruiz and the shadow rapporteurs. our discussions today demonstrate very well the value of effective and continuous dialogue, which i trust will continue as matters progress. i look forward to our future cooperation.
in writing. – health expenditure remains constant even if the prices per patient of some new medicines are higher than in the past. it is true that during the debates on this report, the discussion on affordability of medicines was automatically related to ‘fair price’. but what does fair pricing mean? from my point of view it means one that can reasonably be covered by patients and health budgets and that simultaneously continues to sustain research and development. currently, the high prices of many new medicines are challenging public healthcare systems or patients who have to pay for them out of their own pocket (as is the situation in most low- and middle-income countries). therefore, we have to find solutions to overcome this situation by taking into account the economic circumstances and needs of the health system of each country, not by creating idealistic references for high-income countries in price setting, and highlighting the advantages of incremental innovation. we also need to address the additional barriers which hamper patients’ access to medicines, and which are not related to budgets: red tape and bureaucracy, lack of vision for the medium and long term, instability of legislation in many member states, unpredictability, and a lack of dialogue and partnership.
in writing. it is regrettable that many citizens in the member states do not have access to healthcare or medicines and, moreover, it is extremely worrying that thousands of people are dying because of the lack of effective treatments for rare diseases, as well as because of the lack of access to certain treatments or their astronomical cost. member states should support research and development based on the medical needs of citizens, with the aim of creating innovative medicines and generic medicines at affordable prices for all patients. more transparency is also needed in the cost of investments in pharmaceutical research, development and innovation so that the consumer does not end up paying twice for the same product. i believe that member states should cooperate on their own initiative, in particular as regards prices, reimbursements and exchange of information. i urge public decision-makers to take proactive steps to ensure that generic and biosimilar medicines become available in a timely manner to reduce in a meaningful way the total costs and expenditure for medicines, always taking into account the need to ensure the same benefits and continuity of patient care.
in writing. it is well known that access to healthcare is a fundamental right of all citizens. as such, one of the core goals of the eu and who, namely sustainable development goal 3, is precisely to ensure access to medicines for individuals (patients). obviously, access to medicines is dependent on the timely availability of medicines and their accessibility to all citizens without discrimination. however, there are still major disparities between public health systems, as well as between pharmaceutical systems in the member states, and the challenges posed by the ageing of the eu population. moreover, access to medicines is restricted either by pharmaceutical business strategies (profit maximisation strategies), or for political reasons related to the production or distribution process or even because of parallel trade, or because of lower incomes of some member states. however, improving access to medicines can also be achieved by reducing administrative procedures and budgetary constraints, by developing biosimilars and innovative medicines. the involvement of all stakeholders in the healthcare field (producers, researchers, patient organisations, institutions, etc.) is also essential to improve access to medicines for european citizens.

on behalf of the s&d group. madam president, commissioner, first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the successful conclusion of the negotiations. we are talking about very important new rules that will improve food safety and help to combat practices that pose health risks. the food supply chain is often long and complex. that is why harmonised rules are needed to guarantee the same level of safety for everyone and to simplify this process for all involved. consumers, food producers, traders and authorities will all benefit from simplified standards applied consistently throughout the chain. the new types of controls will be based on risk assessment, thus helping to focus the authorities' attention where it is really needed. the inspections will be unannounced, making it more difficult for operators to hide non-compliant practices from the authorities. tougher penalties will help discourage those companies tempted to resort to food fraud. in addition to ensuring better consumer protection, the new legislation will also help to support those companies that comply with the law. for example, producers of organic food or food with a protected geographical indication, which have often faced unfair competition, will benefit. food safety, food quality, fair competition and consumer confidence are key elements of this new legislation.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in the context of sustainable development, in order to protect and promote food security and the good nutritional status of the citizens of europe, it is necessary to regulate risks to the integrity of humans, animals and plants, through harmonised rules on the identity, health and quality of plant reproductive material, animal by-products, production regulation, veterinary and phytosanitary legislation, but also rules on consumer information and fair trading practices in trade in products in the agri-food chain. of course, the correct and effective application of eu agri-food chain legislation can be established through official controls, carried out in member states and third countries, and a robust but simplified, transparent and sustainable legislative framework for their organisation contributes to the modernisation, integration and efficient functioning of the european union's reliable and coherent control system, thus giving competent authorities access to up-to-date technical data, research results, new techniques and the necessary expertise, as well as the most effective tools for the performance of official controls and other official activities.
mr president, the european union must have as its main objective the improvement of the efficiency of the official control system at member state level, so that throughout the food chain there are high standards of safety and quality which give confidence to the european consumer. at the same time, there is a need to modernise and simplify the instruments to enable the implementation of the legislation and to guarantee real protection of animal and plant health and welfare. the administrative burden on small and micro enterprises should be reduced so that the administrative burden is not transferred to a higher cost of the products being marketed. i also appreciate the need to strengthen official controls on the marketing standards for agricultural products in order to prevent fraudulent and misleading practices, but - and i stress this - also to apply appropriate financial penalties to discourage them. it is of the utmost importance to strengthen alert mechanisms and information exchange between national authorities so that any safety risk in the food chain can be countered by rapid action. at present, there are significant concerns in eastern european countries about the double quality standards of products being marketed compared to western european countries. in other words, we have the same product, the same brand, the same packaging, but a different and inferior quality of the product, which i regard as unacceptable. in this context, it is rightly said that cheese is sometimes made from milk, sausages may contain meat, and wine is occasionally made from grapes. moreover, beyond the mandatory labelling of products, effective mechanisms must be found to expressly prohibit the use of the name 'cheese' or 'meat' if these products do not contain a significant proportion of raw material of animal origin. otherwise, instead of saying "good appetite" when we sit down to eat, we might say "good luck" because we don't know what's on our plate.

rapporteur. – mr president, colleagues, commissioner oettinger, i am bringing to your attention tonight the draft report on the guidelines for the budget of the european union for 2018. it is the report in which we, as a parliament, are putting forward our political priorities for the budget of the union for next year. i would like to propose two political priorities: number one, growth and jobs; and number two, security. i would like to propose these as priorities because these are exactly the areas in which the citizens of the union expect that the union will deliver: number one, growth and jobs; number two, security. how will we achieve this? number one: on growth and jobs, i propose that we invest more in infrastructure, innovation and research, that we support more smes, and that we invest more in entrepreneurs, especially highly innovative entrepreneurs. so programmes like the connecting europe facility, horizon 2020, cosme, erasmus, the european fund for strategic investments (efsi) have to be enforced in the budget of the union for next year, because it is only by strengthening the economy of the union and making it more competitive and more credible in the eyes of investors that it will be able to grow and create jobs. the second priority which i am proposing is security. this has two aspects, two components: internal security and external security. for internal security, as we all know, the financial means under heading 3 are very limited. so the question is: how can we have an impact with the limited financial resources which we have available? i propose that we strengthen the agencies of the union which have responsibilities in the area of justice and home affairs: frontex, easo, europol and eurojust. we need to strengthen them, and we need to make them cooperate better and use synergy effects between them. also, to improve internal security, i support the defence pilot projects launched by the european commission this year. they have to continue because, until now, we have spent money in 28 member states of the union 28 times for defence industries and defence research for the same results. this needs to end where it can. we need to achieve economies of scale. spend money once at european level and share the results, as is normal to do amongst partner countries. security also has an external dimension, and i would like us to stand side-by-side with the eastern neighbourhood of the union and with those countries which have embarked on a pro-european path the three countries that have signed association agreements with the european union: ukraine, georgia and the republic of moldova. they face a more aggressive russian federation. we need to stand by their side to strengthen their institutions, their judiciary – the independence of the judiciary – the rule of law, to fight money laundering and to fight corruption. we also need to stand by the countries in our southern neighbourhood, northern africa and the middle east. these are countries of origin or countries of transit for refugees, and it is for us much cheaper, it is politically easier and it is safer for the union to support refugees in their countries of origin. it is also preferable for them. we can achieve much better results by supporting them there and preventing them from coming in high numbers to europe. these are the main political priorities which i am putting forward for debate and for vote tomorrow. in addition to these, there are also small punctual projects which help different categories of people in europe. we believe in the erasmus programme. it has to be strengthened, but we believe that in addition to the erasmus programme, the interrail project – which was proposed over the course of the past month and which would enable every young citizen in europe who turns 18 to receive from the budget of the union a free 30-day interrail pass – is something which would enable people to learn more about europe, to practice the foreign languages which they have learned in school, and, in particular, to increase their chances of finding a good job. as we know, employers appreciate international experience. on this basis we would like to ask the commission to put forward a legislative proposal to enable the interrail project in a transparent, predictable and sustainable way without, of course, affecting any other existing projects. i thank you for your attention. i am looking forward to the debate tonight.

rapporteur. – madam president, looking back at our common endeavour to get an efficient and workable conflict minerals regulation fulfilling the european parliament mandate as it was adopted in this house, we have been quite successful. first, we have been able to speak with one voice and, second, we have been able to achieve the majority of parliament’s objectives. the vicious circle has now been broken. the importers of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold will have to carry out mandatory due diligence in order to check their suppliers and prevent armed rebels or human rights violations being financed by illegal revenue. the interests of communities and people caught in wars and conflict were our priority. the new regulation has the power to improve reality on the ground in conflict areas. we followed two principles in our work: first to help the people affected by illegal mining and trade conducted by armed groups and, second, to increase the responsibility of all stakeholders, including european industry, in a common effort towards transparency. the recognition of due diligence schemes proposed by industry associations and responsible sourcing partnerships has become the central element of the regulation. all industry initiatives have to fully comply with the international oecd due diligence guidelines elaborated to help companies respect human rights and avoid contributing to conflict financing. it is important that all companies, including those from downstream in the supply chain whose products contain 3tg, will be encouraged to monitor their sources. compulsory checks for the importers will ensure that minerals or metals sold on the european market are not used to illegally finance conflicts, particularly in mineral-rich countries affected by conflicts or war. educating the stakeholders and achieving long-term sustainable effects is only possible through an approach based on shared responsibility. the regulation proposed to you today will be very important in creating good premises for more prosperity in the conflict areas, and this will lead to more stability. stability in africa and all other conflict areas means fewer migration flows to the european union. to protect smes and to minimise bureaucracy and red tape, the regulation offers an exemption for the smallest importers, based on a threshold system designed to cover at least 95% of all imports to the european union. through delegated acts parliament will be able to keep control of the implementation. parliament also ensured that the commission will regularly report on the accompanying measures meant to make the regulation more effective. our aim was to create an efficient and workable regulation and we fully succeeded. now we will carefully monitor the update by the european companies and, if necessary, we will adjust the system, making use of the powerful review clause included in the provisions of the regulation. finally i wish to express my sincerest thanks to all the shadow rapporteurs, the negotiating team members, and all the experts, advisers and staff members involved in this highly technical and very complicated process. i would like to highlight the special support of commissioner cecilia malmström, who personally attended all the negotiating sessions.

member of the commission. – madam president, this is another very important subject. on behalf of vice—president ansip, i would like to thank parliament, and in particular the rapporteur, mr jáuregui atondo, for this report on the subject of e-democracy. it concerns issues that are fundamental to how we evolve as democratic and innovative societies, and it recognises the strategic role that new digital technologies play in shaping public policy and public services. vice-president ansip has asked me to make a number of comments, so i hope you will bear with me. citizens and businesses expect better services from public authorities, greater transparency and less administrative burden. despite many eu projects over the years to develop concepts, tools and solutions for participatory democracy, the pace of modernisation is still too slow. we need to accelerate the transformation of government and improve people’s participation in decision-making processes. if we can use digital technology to support an increased public involvement, that is good for legitimacy, accountability and ultimately trust in government. the new e-government action plan will contribute to this digital transformation. it is part of our broader vision for creating a digital single market. it aims to promote open and transparent government, as well as to improve the interaction of government and individual citizens. governments and administrations need to be open, transparent and collaborative. this means open data, open services and open processes. ict is a great tool to engage people, to improve transparency and to increase the accountability and relevance of public administration. that is why the commission recognises the importance of e-democracy and e-participation. it helps us to make sure our policies respond to individual and business needs and so increases trust in our political systems. the eu citizenship report 2017 underlined the commission’s commitment to promoting best practices to help people vote and stand in eu elections. with european elections in 2019, the aim is to support turnout and broad democratic participation. these best practices should also address e-democracy, remote voting arrangements like e-voting, and cross-border access to political information. they will also focus on improving the low voter turnout. in its report, parliament highlights the importance of all of this and calls for greater eu-wide cooperation, but we also need to recognise the challenges. political parties and elections increasingly attract the attention of cyber criminals and other cyber activists. this risk to our democratic processes is, unfortunately, real and we need to take it very seriously. for the dsm to work, our digital networks have to be protected. that is why cyber security needs to be a top political priority for us all, and it certainly is for the commission. e-democracy also requires equal, open and neutral access to the internet. the commission has always been committed to the internet as a single unfragmented space. our approach continues to be one where the internet is anchored in the defence of human rights and democratic values, where the same rights that apply offline are also protected online. we also need to ensure that everyone can benefit from new opportunities that are presented by the new technologies. recently the web accessibility directive entered into force. this means making the internet accessible for everyone, including the elderly and people with disabilities. but to make the most of internet access and for people to engage digitally, we need wide availability and take-up of high-speed broadband connectivity. that is why the commission has proposed connectivity targets for 2025. one of these is for all european households to have access to download speeds of at least 100 mbps. in addition, given the investment challenge ahead, especially in less densely populated areas, eu cohesion policies complement private investment and support broadband deployment to the tune of some eur 6 billion up to 2020, with a particular focus on under-served and rural areas. for e-democracy to be efficient and thrive, people must also have access to information as well as the necessary skills. at the same time, people who do not have the full means or skills to participate should not be excluded, which is an essential part of building trust. in its communication last year ‘a new skills agenda for europe’, the commission proposed a skills guarantee to help europeans to get more access to basic literacy, numeracy and digital skills training. we also work with member states under the education and training 2020 initiative to bring more digital skills to students and into school and university curricula. lastly, let us remember the importance of media pluralism and freedom of expression, values that are enshrined in the charter. they are the backbone of our democratic societies whether people are online or offline. media literacy is a key factor for people to make the most of the unprecedented amount of data information and views that they can now access thanks to digital technologies. so once again thank you to the rapporteur for raising these subjects in an interesting and important report, and thank you for the opportunity to discuss them so fully this evening.

in writing. – the eu renewable energy policy is driving demand for biofuels within and beyond europe’s borders. this has led to massive land-use change in various parts of the world and can have serious consequences. the competition for arable land has affected food security at local level as well as global food prices. some biofuels can even emit more greenhouse gases than the fossil fuels they were supposed to replace. given these concerns, i welcome the measures proposed in this report. a phasing out of palm oil will reduce the risk of associated deforestation and damaging land-use change. and certification based on sustainability criteria will reduce demand for the most damaging biofuels. bio-based fuels are not infinite natural resources which can be exploited without consequences. over-exploitation requires huge amounts of land, water, fertilisers and pesticides, causing pollution, soil degradation, and damage to ecosystem services. a bio-based economy must be developed in the right way, because using the wrong sources of bio-energy can do far more harm than good.
in writing. the 2030 agenda commits the european union to promote sustainable forest management by halting deforestation, restoring degraded forests and substantially increasing afforestation and reforestation. this is possible by providing sustainable production and consumption patterns and practices to both businesses and consumers, in line with national policies and priorities. at the same time, palm oil consumption, expected to double by 2050, is driving deforestation of tropical forests, which means the destruction of natural habitats, ecosystems and biodiversity, as well as climate change. moreover, the production of palm oil infringes the fundamental rights and freedoms of those involved in that process. palm oil (dende), the most widely used in the food industry, is also carcinogenic, according to the european union's european food safety authority (efsa). as such, there is a need to intensify research and awareness-raising campaigns on the impact of the use and consumption of palm oil on human health and safety and on the environment, as well as research into the social dimension of the production, use and consumption of palm oil.

madam president, the title of this debate has struck me, because when we talk about fake news, we are simply talking about lies. i'm afraid we must not be afraid to call things by their right names. the practice of hate speech, populist arguments and lies is not new. i come from a country that has had this experience under communism. what is new is indeed the use of social media. otherwise, the objective of terrorist groups and extremist political parties is the same as that of totalitarian regimes in the past, namely to establish authoritarian regimes and thus to revive totalitarian practices. the attacks that have brutally struck europe have made us aware of the need to work together to counter terrorist propaganda. the task is not easy because, despite the goodwill of social media companies, it is very difficult to identify such messages and remove them in time. the european union has made a significant effort with the establishment of the stratcom task force to combat the hate messages of the islamic state group, but for our actions to have a real impact, we need to provide this structure with real means. a few months ago we adopted a report on the union's strategic communication in this area and one thing is clear: effective communication will not be enough, we must invest in education, awareness-raising and, above all, in freedom of the press. this freedom is essential to fight against these lies.
in writing. – fake news or, as it likes to call itself, ‘alternative news’, is not news. yet today the scale of this phenomenon is astounding. how does it sustain itself? let’s follow the money! journalists found fake news websites, fake products, promoted by fake photos, fake names and fake statements and advertising agencies. all of them getting real money from gullible readers and buyers and all connected through ownership. we are talking about a huge audience and a system that produces countless financial resources. underneath there is a whole machinery which goes much deeper than just a room with internet trolls, somewhere in moscow. are we worried? apparently some of us are not. someone asked here today: ‘who can have the authority to say what is true and what is false’. this gives credit to something that is both junk and malicious. later i heard ‘who has the right to remove or censor the information’. a piece of junk becomes ‘information’ and later ‘freedom of speech and opinion’. that is both irresponsible and dangerous. the eu must build, as soon as possible, an institutional and legal framework capable to create the specific antibodies needed to protect european citizens from this disease.
in writing. hate speech, populism and fake news are three phenomena that have seen a worrying rise in recent years. eu citizens are increasingly exposed to disinformation and propaganda campaigns, and as we have already seen with brexit, they seem to be working. this should concern us and we should take a firm stand against those who deliberately misinform. as we approach two very important elections in france and germany, it is important that we remain vigilant and not allow the debates to be hijacked by people and organizations that are betting on hate and fear to win. we need to punish hate speech, including anti-semitism and anti-islamism, and fake news, drastically. at the same time, in order to prevent the spread of false information, i support the strengthening of media institutions so that they are objective, impartial and independent. i express my support for investments in all member states to raise awareness and education, including the use of digital platforms. this would allow citizens to critically analyse the media content and information they access on the internet, contributing to personal, national and european security.
in writing. in the era of 'post-truth', as some have summarised the historic moment we are living through due to the instrumentalisation of the internet, it is becoming a priority for the eu to combat fake news, so-called alternative sources of information and the propaganda avalanche. as a rule, the information chaos and media intoxication work in the interest of extremist, anti-european forces hostile to the integration and peaceful project of the european union. social media is the main source of information for a third of young europeans. that is why illegal content online, fake news and hate speech must be tackled firmly and effectively. human, technical and financial resources appropriate to the scale of the challenge are required. and in this regard, i draw attention to two major crises that have been fuelled by new technologies: the recruitment of jihadists and the coordination of terrorist attacks by the islamic state, and the information war launched by russia against the eu. combating hostile propaganda and providing citizens with accurate information are strategic obligations in this hostile context.

in writing. the debate on 'wholesale roaming' is natural in the context of the european union's aim to eliminate roaming charges by 15 june 2017. we, the policy-makers, must take the interests of the citizens first and foremost into account, and at this moment the interest of european citizens is to have zero costs when travelling to any member state. citizens want to see the european union take more interest and propose more concrete solutions to their everyday problems, sometimes even at the expense of their private or national interests. national wholesale roaming markets should therefore be competitive and offer wholesale roaming charges that allow operators to offer retail roaming services in a sustainable manner without additional costs. the solution i propose is to regulate all aspects of wholesale roaming at european level, either by keeping the current tariffs or by deciding together to substantially reduce them, with the main aim of completely eliminating costs for ordinary citizens by implementing the 'roam like at home' (rlah) rules.

president of the eurogroup. – madam president, first of all, many members of parliament have been very critical about my remarks in the interviews, and of course i fully accept that. the choice of words was unfortunate and people have been offended, and i regret that. the underlying debate still remains valid: that to build a community requires everyone to take responsibility, respecting agreements and frameworks, and, on that basis, moving forward together and strengthening solidarity in the union and in the eurozone. that is the legacy that i would like to leave. that is what i have worked for and i think, looking back on the last four and a half years, the eurozone is in a much better state than when i came to the job as we are moving out of the crisis and many member states are back into strong growth. i stress again that my remarks were about the responsibility for all member states, not some of them, and if the impression was that it was about some of them, i regret that. it was not my intention. i believe that all of us should take that responsibility. i will make one remark about my personal opinions on the development of the european stability mechanism (esm): i believe it can play a stronger role, which would also allow the imf not to be part of future programmes. i am not excluding them from being part of future programmes and i certainly hope we won’t need any future programmes, but i feel that the esm can play a leading role and that it should develop in that direction. that does not mean that i wish to take away responsibilities from the commission. i made my remark about the commission to underline that i feel that the commission should stay in the lead as the guardian of the pact and the rules that we share. finally, on greece, parliament has my personal strong commitment that we will achieve that deal for greece in may. it needs to be done in may. we have put in a lot of effort. the situation in greece is not good enough; growth is falling back again where we need trust and growth to continue. so, yes, you have my personal commitment and i will come back to parliament as soon as possible with that fair deal for greece. i believe that, already in the package we are discussing now, the emphasis is not on austerity; it is about deep reforms that are necessary to create more growth, and any fiscal outcome of that can be reinvested in greece and used for the positive policy initiatives so badly needed in greece. finally, yes, we will discuss debt, and debt relief will be needed to find that solution. that is my opinion, and i believe that is shared in the eurogroup. last year we already gave that commitment to come back to the issue of sustainability of debt for greece, because that is the only way that they will come back onto a sustainable path and a sustainable economic future.
in writing. again, greece is on the edge with its external debt due in july 2017, in the absence of an agreement with the international monetary fund, the european financial stability facility and the european commission. this situation has been repeatedly repeated in recent years. the reason is very clear: the creditors do not want to take their share of responsibility for allowing greece's external debt to reach unusual dimensions (currently 180 percent of greece's gross domestic product). in fact, a fundamental condition for any restructuring of a country's external debt is not met: the achievement of a new balance between the country's real potential to generate revenue (after the adoption of reforms) and the debt due in future years. in the case of greece, the need to write off part of the debt is clear. the creditors are resisting, but eventually they'll have to accept that truth.

on behalf of the alde group. – madam president, we are living in a world that changes every day and facing constant technological challenges that demand the continuous development of knowledge, skills and competence. both the private and the public sector require skills that were almost unconceivable 30 years ago, and in adapting to these changes we should no longer follow old-school ways when it comes to education. yet our education and training systems lag behind this new dynamic, limiting the recognition of non-formal and informal learning, including the skills gained during volunteering activities. this is damaging, not only in relation to a short-term economic outcome, but also to the main aim of education: generating adaptable and independent individuals able to face the challenges ahead with open minds and confidence. greater flexibility in skills recognition is beneficial for european citizens, and can also lead to better economic and social integration for migrants and refugees, thus responding to another challenge of the eu. at the same time, through structured dialogues with the eu neighbourhood countries, especially the ones that have an association agreement with the eu, we should aim at referencing their national qualification frameworks to the european training foundation. in this way, if sooner or later these countries become eu members, their citizens will be ready to cope with the demands of the european markets and labour force from day one. moreover, eu support through development aid should be directed to third countries in order to offer assistance in developing national qualifications frameworks. the revision of the european qualifications framework should result in an innovative meta-framework that responds to all these existing challenges but also think ahead, anticipate potential problems and offers ‘out of the box’ solutions.
madam president, although the european qualifications framework has been a significant driver of reforms in the setup of national frameworks, as the commission is also aware, not all the objectives of the 2008 recommendation were reached in terms of comparability and portability of qualifications. this is why, if we take european cross-border mobility of learners and workers and lifelong learning seriously, it is important that we make qualifications more transparent and understandable across different countries and different educational systems. one of the greatest challenges in referencing national systems in a common framework is posed by the changes over time in qualification systems. this makes it necessary to keep referencing activity constant and up to date, especially considering the increasing proliferation of international sectoral, industry-based training and certifications. i would especially welcome if the commission could provide more details on this.
member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the house for today’s debate that shows the importance we all attach to the european qualifications framework (eqf). i will not go into the details of your questions one by one, but i would like to stress that the eqf is a tool to make skills and qualifications more transparent. it is not about automatic recognition or the harmonisation of national qualifications frameworks. secondly, the eqf revision builds on the achievements of the recommendation of 2008, and it will make the eqf a more effective tool adapted to the reality of today and to the evolving nature of qualifications. and finally, the future success of the eqf is in the hands of member states and stakeholders, who are in charge of implementation. the commission’s role will be one of support. i count on your continued support for the eqf and for other initiatives within the european skills agenda. it is our joint responsibility to offer citizens the necessary tools to develop their skills and find the jobs that are right for them. this counts especially for the still more than 19 million unemployed people in our union. skills are of the utmost importance for them, so we are working on this, including by improving the eqf. this is only one of our actions to create more jobs, more growth and fairness in our union.
in writing. the european qualifications framework for lifelong learning is a crucial tool for improving the employability and mobility of european citizens. we live in a constantly changing world where the demands of the labour market are increasing, requiring rapid and continuous adaptation of knowledge, skills and abilities. unfortunately, education systems are not following this dynamic and the recognition of non-formal and informal learning outcomes is still very limited, negatively impacting on the employment and career opportunities of a significant part of the population, especially for people from vulnerable groups. i therefore believe that the review of this qualifications framework must also take into account the increased visibility and importance of skills acquired outside the classroom, which will facilitate equal opportunities in a more open, tolerant and inclusive europe.
mr. president, the data we have on food waste is shocking. 88 million tonnes of food were wasted in the european union in 2012, and globally almost a third of food ends up in landfills. the real cost is huge because it reflects the costs involved in producing food with energy, water, transportation, fertilizer and everything that holds the soil. equally high are the associated costs: carbon emissions, water pollution, degradation of soil and ecosystems. all of these are consequences of overproduction. food waste only stimulates this overproduction, which over time diminishes the ability of agricultural land to provide food for a growing population in the future. as my colleagues have said, it's also a moral and political issue, not just a dietary one. enormous amounts of food are wasted, while a very large number of europeans, including children, are facing poverty and malnutrition. the resolution tabled by the environment committee makes some important and practical proposals, and work has already begun on common definitions and methodologies to combat this phenomenon. i call on my colleagues to support these proposals, as well as the mandatory measures proposed to be applied at european union level that are necessary to combat food waste along the entire food chain.
in writing. the target of reducing food waste by 30% by 2025 and by 50% by 2030 (compared to 2014 levels) cannot be achieved without the involvement of all actors in the food supply chain and without relevant analyses of the causes of food waste and identification of the food sectors with the highest food waste, with a view to identifying solutions to prevent it. i welcome the rapporteur's proposal to involve national authorities and industry partners in carrying out information campaigns to help consumers understand the best before and use by labels. in this context, i consider it useful to involve the eu platform on food loss and food waste in supporting the implementation of consumer food information and education programmes, facilitating cooperation of local stakeholders in food waste prevention and food donation initiatives, and evaluating good practices already implemented in different member states in order to better define effective tools to reduce food waste.
in writing. while some people (around 800 million people globally) barely have enough to eat, others can afford to throw away kilograms of food periodically, generating unprecedented, immoral and unethical food waste. as such, all stakeholders (institutions, organisations, households, industries, traders, distributors, research institutes, etc.) must contribute to combating food loss and reducing waste. the united nations sustainable development goal of halving food waste by 2030 can be achieved by the combined efforts of all the actors involved in this major environmental impact phenomenon and by a holistic approach to all relevant policies at union and member state level. reducing waste and improving food security can be the direct result of changing the consumption behaviour of the population, through a process of empowering each individual, and information and persuasion are absolutely necessary to this end. limiting food losses can be achieved through the use of economic and fiscal incentives to facilitate the donation of safe and edible food. a clear definition of food waste also leads to its recovery as a safe feed resource.
